tldr: When manipulating deformable objects, it is not enough to simply complete the task—we must also avoid crushing them. Yet, conventional benchmarks overlook this physical interaction quality. This work introduces SoftVTBench, a benchmark pairing synchronized visuo-tactile observations with FEM physical deformation ground truth, enabling precise policy evaluation through a new metric called DSR that requires both task completion and staying within deformation limits.
hero_caption: Overview of SoftVTBench. It features 4,000 episodes across four evaluation suites and over 50 assets (volumetric deformable objects and visually matched rigid twins). It synchronizes visual, tactile, language, and action streams alongside evaluator-only FEM deformation states. As illustrated at the bottom center, it quantitatively evaluates contact quality across the full spectrum from loose, slipping grasps to excessive compression.
overview:
When a robot handles delicate deformable objects like bread, fresh produce, or medical supplies, moving an item to the target location is still a failure if the robot crushes it along the way. However, most existing robotic manipulation benchmarks evaluate models solely on task success rate—whether the object reached the goal. This gap exists because no prior dataset paired policy-visible contact observations with independent physical ground-truth deformation across complete tasks.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed SoftVTBench, a deformation-aware visuo-tactile dataset and benchmark. Built in Isaac Sim using finite-element method (FEM) simulation, it pre-calibrates object-specific deformation tolerances: the threshold beyond which an object is considered crushed. While the robot receives multi-view camera feeds and dual-finger GelSight-style tactile data (RGB images and marker displacements), the simulator synchronously records all FEM nodal deformations behind the scenes. This enables a new evaluation metric, the Deformation-aware Success Rate (DSR), which requires both completing the task and staying within the deformation limit.

Evaluating three representative policy families—Diffusion Policy, the VLA model $\pi_{0.5}$, and the world model FastWAM—revealed that up to 24% of rollouts considered successful under standard metrics actually caused excessive deformation. Furthermore, while adding touch showed mixed benefits in-distribution (ID), it consistently enhanced robustness under distribution shifts (OOD) such as novel lighting or modified physical properties. These findings shed light on the true value of tactile sensing and the ongoing challenges of multimodal fusion.
contributions: Released a dataset of 4,000 expert demonstrations across 40 deformable-object manipulation tasks, synchronizing multi-view vision, dual-finger touch (RGB and marker motion), robot proprioception, language, actions, and evaluator-only FEM deformation ground truth at 20 Hz.
Introduced the Deformation-aware Success Rate (DSR), an evaluation metric that simultaneously assesses task completion and deformation limits based on pre-calibrated object-specific tolerances.

Established an experimental protocol featuring visually and mass-matched rigid twins as well as discrete and continuous gripper actions, isolating the effects of object deformability and control granularity.

Evaluated three modern policy families, empirically demonstrating that task-success-only metrics overlook excessive deformation and showing the strengths and challenges of tactile sensing under out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts.

sections.heading: Did It Succeed If It Crushed the Object? The Missing Physical Ground Truth in Deformable Manipulation
sections.summary: Existing benchmarks focus almost entirely on task completion, overlooking poor contact quality like slipping or excessive compression. This work presents SoftVTBench, which provides tactile inputs to policies while independently tracking FEM physical deformation ground truth, introducing the DSR metric to evaluate both task success and gentle handling.
sections.details:
Imagine a robot grasping a soft piece of bread or fruit to place it in a basket. If the object slips from its fingers, that is clearly a failure. However, if the robot squeezes the object with excessive force and places it in the basket, conventional metrics judge the attempt as a success simply because the object reached the target area. Such an evaluation falls short for delicate applications in food handling or healthcare.

While vision is well suited for reaching toward objects and verifying goals, the contact surface becomes occluded during grasping. Tactile sensing is therefore crucial for capturing contact geometry, local slip, and shear forces directly. Validating touch, however, requires a deliberate data design: policy-visible streams (vision, touch, proprioception, language, and actions) must be separated from an evaluator-only stream (the object's true deformation state) while maintaining strict synchronization throughout the task. Raw tactile sensor readouts cannot serve as an unbiased ground-truth label for object deformation.

To address this limitation, this paper introduces SoftVTBench, comprising 40 pick-and-place tasks, over 50 assets, and 4,000 expert demonstrations. By computing the net deformation from 3D FEM meshes with rigid-body motion removed, the benchmark defines the Deformation-aware Success Rate (DSR), measuring whether tasks finish without exceeding pre-calibrated tolerances. Experiments across representative policies reveal severe, previously hidden deformation violations among successful rollouts.

sections.heading: General Manipulation, Deformable Objects, and Tactile Learning: What Prior Benchmarks Missed
sections.summary: While research has advanced across robot manipulation, deformable object simulation, and visuo-tactile policy learning, no single benchmark has brought all three together. SoftVTBench is the first benchmark to combine complete multi-stage tasks, volumetric 3D deformable assets, policy tactile inputs, and evaluator-only deformation ground truth.
sections.details:
This section categorizes prior work into three main threads:

- **Robot manipulation benchmarks**: Suites such as LIBERO, RoboCasa, and SIMPLER have standardized multi-stage language-conditioned tasks and generalization assessments. Some benchmarks incorporate safety metrics, but they focus almost exclusively on rigid objects and cannot directly measure how much a deformable object compresses.
- **Deformable-object benchmarks**: Platforms like SoftGym and PlasticineLab simulate deformable materials such as cloth, rope, or plasticine, but their primary objective is typically shape alteration. In contrast, this paper focuses on gentle handling—transporting objects without damaging them. While a few studies measure deformation during grasping, they are limited to isolated static grasps rather than closed-loop tactile policies over complete manipulation tasks.
- **Visuo-tactile sensing and policy learning**: With simulators like Taxim and TacEx, optical tactile sensing (including GelSight) has become popular for policy learning and VLA models. Yet, these works evaluate success primarily on rigid-object tasks, and force-measuring studies typically track rigid-surface contact forces.

As shown in the paper's comparison (Table 1), no prior benchmark simultaneously satisfied all four criteria: complete tasks, 3D volumetric deformable assets, tactile policy inputs, and evaluator-only deformation ground truth. SoftVTBench is the first to integrate them.

sections.heading: Designing the Dataset: Decoupling Tactile Rendering from FEM Ground-Truth Streams
sections.summary: Built in Isaac Sim, the dataset contains 4,000 expert demonstrations. Alongside third-person and wrist camera images, dual-finger GelSight data, and control commands, nodal FEM coordinates are synchronously recorded at 20 Hz, paired with pre-calibrated safe grasp zones for each object.
sections.details:
The dataset architecture and collection procedure are carefully structured:

### 3.1 Dataset Organization
The dataset is divided equally across four suites (10 tasks and 1,000 demonstrations each): Object-Soft, Spatial-Soft, Object-Rigid, and Spatial-Rigid. The assets include ten volumetric deformable objects: six realistic food meshes (such as bread) and four geometric primitives. Crucially, each asset has a visually matched rigid twin that shares the exact geometry, texture, and mass, isolating whether manipulation difficulties stem from deformability itself.

### 3.2 Decoupling Observation and Evaluation Streams
All observations and actions are logged synchronously at 20 Hz. The policy-visible stream contains third-person and wrist RGB images, dual-finger GelSight Mini data (optical images and marker motion simulated via TacEx), proprioception (gripper pose and joint positions), natural language instructions, and gripper commands (both discrete binary and continuous). In contrast, the evaluator-only stream records FEM nodal coordinates, object poses, and contact events, remaining strictly inaccessible during training and inference.

### 3.3–3.5 Scene Generation, Quality Control, and Calibration
Expert trajectories are generated via scripted policies and pass both physical verification and human visual inspection. Deformation is measured by computing the root-mean-square (RMS) displacement across all FEM nodes relative to the undeformed mesh, removing rigid-body translation and rotation, and normalizing by the initial bounding-box diagonal. Before policy training, physical grasp sweeps identify the safe grasp range $\mathcal{G}_o=[g^{\min}_o, g^{\max}_o]$—from the minimum width required to lift without slip to the limit before excessive deformation—and establish the deformation tolerance $\tau_o$ (the 90th percentile of maximum deformation during stable grasps). Fixing these parameters beforehand ensures an unbiased, stable evaluation metric.

sections.heading: How DSR Separates Task Success from Physical Safety
sections.summary: Policies execute closed-loop control at 20 Hz, predicting actions from multi-view vision and touch. In addition to the standard Task Success Rate (TSR), the benchmark defines the Deformation-aware Success Rate (DSR), which counts a rollout as successful only when the maximum normalized deformation remains within tolerance $\tau_o$.
sections.details:
The benchmark execution and evaluation protocol are structured as follows:

### 4.1 Closed-Loop Evaluation Interface
During evaluation, the simulator passes only the policy-visible stream (vision, proprioception, language, and touch) to the policy. The policy outputs action chunks consisting of absolute end-effector poses and gripper commands, which are executed in closed-loop physical simulation. Episodes run for up to 300 steps and terminate early upon success or dropped objects. Meanwhile, the simulator continuously reads out ground-truth FEM nodal positions in the background.

### 4.2 Formulating the Deformation-aware Success Rate (DSR)
Let $T_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denote binary task success for episode $i$ (whether the target object comes to rest in the goal region). Let $D_{i,t}$ be the rigid-body-invariant RMS deformation at time $t$. The normalized deformation relative to the object tolerance $\tau_{o_i}$ is $R_t^{(i)} = D_{i,t} / \tau_{o_i}$, with peak value $R_{\max}^{(i)} = \max_t R_t^{(i)}$.

Task Success Rate (TSR) and Deformation-aware Success Rate (DSR) are then computed as:

$$\mathrm{TSR} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N T_i$$
$$\mathrm{DSR} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N T_i \cdot \mathbb{I}\left(R_{\max}^{(i)} \leq 1\right)$$

DSR requires both completing the task and keeping the peak normalized deformation within tolerance ($R_{\max} \leq 1$) throughout the rollout. Consequently, the gap $\mathrm{TSR} - \mathrm{DSR}$ directly captures the fraction of rollouts that completed the task while dangerously crushing the object.

### 4.3 Evaluation Protocol (ID and OOD)
Evaluations cover both in-distribution settings (ID: 500 episodes per suite within training parameter bounds) and out-of-distribution settings (OOD: 900 episodes per suite). OOD evaluations test single-factor variations across nine conditions: three lighting variations, four mass multipliers (1.25$\times$ to 2.5$\times$), and two Young's modulus multipliers (0.5$\times$ and 2.0$\times$).

sections.heading: Experimental Results: 24% of Successful Grasps Over-Deform Objects, and Where Touch Truly Matters
sections.summary: Evaluating Diffusion Policy, $\pi_{0.5}$, and FastWAM revealed consistent gaps between TSR and DSR across all settings, with up to 24% of successful rollouts exceeding deformation limits. While tactile sensing yielded mixed gains in-distribution, it significantly boosted robustness under out-of-distribution (OOD) environmental shifts.
sections.details:
This section addresses five core benchmark questions with empirical data:

- **Unchecked deformation in successful rollouts (Section 5.1)**: Across all 12 deformable ID configurations, DSR was strictly lower than TSR. For Diffusion Policy (visuo-tactile with continuous control), TSR reached 40.0% with a DSR of 30.4% in Object-Soft (a 9.6-point drop) and TSR reached 33.2% with a DSR of 25.2% in Spatial-Soft (an 8.0-point drop). A full 24% of its successful rollouts exceeded the deformation limit.
- **Policy differences in contact regulation (Section 5.2)**: Susceptibility to over-deformation varied substantially by architecture. While Diffusion Policy violated tolerances in 10–24% of its successes and $\pi_{0.5}$ in 8–20%, the world-model-based FastWAM kept violations down to 0.7–6.5%. On the spatial suite, FastWAM showed a gap of only 0.4 points (2 out of 500 rollouts), demonstrating that policies can achieve high success rates while gently regulating contact.
- **The cost of compliance via rigid twins (Section 5.3)**: Compared to rigid twins, $\pi_{0.5}$ suffered an 18.4-point drop in TSR on soft objects, whereas Diffusion Policy and FastWAM dropped by only a few points. In some cases, task complexity or spatial reasoning bottlenecks dominate; the rigid twins isolate these confounding factors from compliance.
- **Tactile sensing vs. control granularity (Section 5.4)**: For $\pi_{0.5}$, switching from discrete binary control (VO-B) to continuous control (VO-C) with vision alone improved TSR by 11.4 points—matching the 10.8-point gain from adding touch to binary control (VT-B). Evaluating touch without controlling for actuation granularity can easily lead researchers to mistake continuous control gains for tactile benefits.
- **When touch matters most (Section 5.5)**: In-distribution, adding tactile sensing yielded mixed performance. Under distribution shift (OOD), however, visuo-tactile variants (VT-C) outperformed vision-only variants (VO-C) in TSR across all six policy-suite comparisons (sign test $p=0.016$) and achieved higher DSR in five of six. Rather than simply raising peak ID scores, touch provides critical robustness when lighting or object dynamics shift.

captions.F4: Task Success Rate (TSR) under out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. Across variations in lighting, mass, and Young's modulus—particularly in the Spatial-Soft suite (bottom row)—visuo-tactile models (solid red) consistently outperform vision-only models (dashed blue), illustrating touch-driven robustness.

sections.heading: Toward a New Standard for Evaluating Contact Quality
sections.summary: SoftVTBench unites visuo-tactile learning with physical interaction benchmarking. By requiring policies to respect deformation limits alongside task completion, it uncovers physical damage hidden behind conventional success metrics and highlights multimodal fusion as an active research challenge.
sections.details:
In conclusion, the authors provide SoftVTBench: 4,000 expert demonstrations, over 50 assets, rigid twins, and synchronized multimodal observations paired with FEM deformation ground truth. Through the new DSR metric, it exposes the phenomenon of task success accompanied by excessive deformation, which prior benchmarks overlooked.

A key takeaway is that simply feeding tactile sensor data into a policy does not automatically guarantee gentle contact regulation. The modest in-distribution gains of touch indicate that effective visuo-tactile fusion remains an open modeling challenge. At the same time, FastWAM's ability to maintain high task success with under 1% deformation violations proves that this trade-off can be resolved with thoughtful model and control design. SoftVTBench serves as a common resource for investigating not just whether a robot succeeds, but how it physically interacts with deformable objects.

sections.heading: Appendix: Simulation Setup, Qualitative Rollout Comparisons, and Sim-to-Real Considerations
sections.summary: The appendix details the FEM implementation in Isaac Sim with PhysX 5, object-specific calibration parameters, and baseline training configurations. It also provides qualitative rollout visualizations of deformation traces and discusses the scope and limitations of simulated touch for Sim-to-Real transfer.
sections.details:
The appendix provides supplementary information supporting the implementation and analysis:

### Simulation and Calibration Details
The simulation is implemented in Isaac Sim 4.5.0 / Isaac Lab 0.41.3 using the PhysX 5 GPU FEM pipeline at 60 Hz, decimated by 3 to provide 20 Hz policy execution. Deformable assets are modeled as corotational linear elastic soft bodies. Safe grasp widths $\mathcal{G}_o$ and normalized deformation tolerances $\tau_o$ were measured through preliminary grasp sweeps and are released alongside the dataset.

### Qualitative Rollout Comparisons (Figure 5)
Visualizations trace third-person views, wrist views, tactile images, marker displacements, and normalized deformation $R_t$ over time. While camera images look nearly identical, safe rollouts keep $R_{\max} \leq 1$, whereas failing rollouts exhibit sharp spikes in $R_t$ immediately after contact, carrying and placing the object in a heavily crushed state.

### Scope and Limitations of Tactile Simulation
Tactile RGB images are rendered via Taxim and marker displacements via FOTS inside the TacEx plugin for Isaac Sim. While these methods have demonstrated Sim-to-Real transfer in prior literature, the authors note that SoftVTBench's specific assets and contact conditions have not undergone direct real-world calibration. The benchmark focuses on simulated visuo-tactile policy learning, leaving physical Sim-to-Real transfer for future work.

captions.F5: Rollout visualizations across three deformable assets. The top four rows (blue) show gentle successes that stay within deformation limits (DSR=1). The bottom two rows (orange) show rollouts that complete the task (TSR=1) but crush the object at grasp, exceeding the deformation limit $R_t=1$ (DSR=0).

takeaways: Look beyond task success: In deformable-object manipulation, up to 24% of successful rollouts exceeded safe deformation limits and crushed the object. Metrics like DSR that evaluate contact quality are essential.

Touch shines under distribution shift (OOD): While adding touch provides mixed benefits in-distribution (ID), it provides statistically significant robustness when lighting, mass, or compliance change unexpectedly.

Watch out for actuation confounds: Switching from discrete to continuous grasping can yield performance gains comparable to adding tactile sensing; actuation granularity must be controlled when isolating the impact of touch.
Gentle contact is achievable: World-model-based policies like FastWAM demonstrate that high task success rates can coexist with deformation violation rates under 1%.
limitations: Sim-to-Real tactile gap: Although GelSight RGB rendering and marker tracking follow established simulation pipelines, real-world sensor calibration and Sim-to-Real transfer have not yet been validated on SoftVTBench's deformable assets.

Operational definition of deformation limits (DSR): Tolerances $\tau_o$ are derived empirically from simulation grasp sweeps rather than from physical material failure or biological tissue damage thresholds.

Discrepancies in training hyperparameters: Due to GPU memory constraints when ingesting tactile streams, effective batch sizes differed between vision-only and visuo-tactile models for certain baselines, introducing potential optimization confounds.
